paragraphs.heading: What a beach is
paragraphs.text: A beach is a stretch of loose particles lying beside a body of water. The particles usually come from rock, as sand, gravel, shingle or pebbles, or from living things, as mollusc shells or coralline algae. Most beaches sit on coasts, where waves or currents drop sediment and rework it. Lakes and large rivers have beaches too.

paragraphs.heading: The parts near the water
paragraphs.text: A beach has several clear parts, tied to the processes that form and shape it. The beach berm is the part that sits mostly above water, depending on the tide, and that waves act on at some point in the tide. It is the deposit of material that makes up the active shoreline. The berm has a crest, its top, and a face, the slope running from the crest down towards the water. A trough may lie at the face's lowest point. Further out to sea there may be one or more longshore bars, slightly raised underwater banks formed where the waves first begin to break.

paragraphs.heading: Where waves stop and wind takes over
paragraphs.text: Sand may reach well inland from the berm crest. There may be signs there of one or more older crests, called the storm beach, left by very large storm waves and lying beyond the reach of normal waves. At some point waves, even storm waves, stop affecting the beach material. If the particles are sand size or smaller, wind shapes the feature from there. Where wind is what spreads the grains inland, the deposit lying behind the beach turns into a dune. Together these features make up the beach profile.

paragraphs.heading: A shape that changes with the seasons
paragraphs.text: The beach profile changes with the seasons, as wave energy differs between summer and winter months. In temperate areas, summer brings calmer seas and longer gaps between breaking wave crests, and the profile is higher. Gentle waves tend to move sediment up the beach to the berm, and there it is dropped and stays as the water recedes. Onshore winds take it further inland, forming and enhancing dunes. In the storm season, winter in temperate areas, the profile is lower. Higher energy waves breaking in quick succession tend to lift sediment from the shallows and keep it suspended, where it is liable to be swept along the beach by longshore currents or taken out to sea to form longshore bars.

paragraphs.heading: Where beach ends and dune begins
paragraphs.text: The line between beach and dune is hard to pin down in the field. Over any significant stretch of time, sediment is always passing between the two. One possible marker is the drift line, the high point of material left by waves. Normal waves do not wet the sand beyond it, so this would be where significant wind movement of sand could occur. The drift line is likely to move inland, though, when storm waves strike.

paragraphs.heading: Why beaches matter
paragraphs.text: Sandy beaches take up about one third of the world's coastlines. They are popular for recreation and often drive local tourism industries. Preserved beaches are important biomes, serving for example as places where sea turtles breed or where seabirds or penguins nest. With their dunes they also matter for protecting inland ecosystems and human infrastructure from extreme weather. People have changed beaches significantly across the globe, directly through bad building practices on dunes and coastlines, and indirectly through polluted water, plastic pollution, and coastal erosion that comes from sea level rise and climate change. By some estimates, as much as half of the earth's sandy beaches could disappear by 2100 because of sea level rise driven by climate change.
